comparison: Perfect agreement on temporal analysis claims (C23-C27). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find the live imaging data convincing and support the conclusion that synapses form normally before undergoing progressive retraction. Peer reviewers specifically praise the use of 'multiple and complementary approaches including live-imaging.'

Perfect agreement on electrophysiology claims (C28-C29). Both evaluations accept the structure-function correlation data showing intact synapses have normal transmission while retracted synapses lack transmission. Peer reviewers treat these functional data as valid supporting evidence without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on the main conclusion (C69). Both evaluations support the overall model that neural lamella defects lead to axonal degeneration and subsequent synaptic retraction. The editor specifically notes the authors 'provide convincing data identifying and describing the cellular sequence from ECM perturbations to axonal and synaptic degeneration.'

Strong agreement on Perlecan localization (C5, C7-C9). Both evaluations find the localization data convincing. OpenEval notes the imaging provides strong support despite lack of synaptic enrichment contrasting with EM data. Peer reviewers describe the localization as 'convincing' without questioning the findings.

Strong agreement on synaptic retraction phenotype (C11, C13-C19). Both evaluations affirm the core findings with quantitative imaging and genetic validation. Peer reviewers state the authors 'very convincingly demonstrate that in the absence of Perlecan synaptic terminals degenerate' and note the 'drastic increase in synaptic retractions.'

Agreement on cell-type-specific manipulation findings (C33-C38) but with different emphasis. OpenEval highlights this as a key mechanistic insight showing non-cell autonomous function. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data but emphasize the limitation that 'the precise source of Perlecan...remains still unresolved.'

Disagreement on Wg signaling independence (C21-C22). OpenEval finds the genetic interaction data provide 'strong evidence' that the phenotype is independent of Wg signaling. Peer reviewers express concern, stating 'important controls for these negative results are lacking' and the editor notes negative results 'should be strengthened with the addition of appropriate controls.'

Agreement on mechanical stress findings (C40-C41). Both evaluations accept the negative results from hypercontraction experiments. OpenEval acknowledges caveats about retracted NMJs lacking transmission. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings and accept them as part of the rationale for focusing on neural lamella effects.

Agreement on coordinated hemisegment-level phenotype (C44-C45). Both evaluations support the finding that NMJs within hemisegments show similar phenotypes. Peer reviewers note 'the precise correlation of these phenotypes' revealed the cause is 'likely the disruption of the neural lamella,' accepting the coordinated nature.

Strong agreement on neural lamella defects (C46-C47, C49-C50). Both evaluations find the Vkg imaging data convincing. Peer reviewers state the authors 'convincingly demonstrate that the absence of Perlecan...causes a severe perturbation of the ECM-based neural lamella' and accept that defects precede retraction.

Agreement on axonal pathology and temporal sequence (C58-C63). Both evaluations support the developmental time-course showing progressive axonal damage. Peer reviewers note 'axons and even entire nerve bundles break at sites prior to the innervation' and accept the temporal analysis as valid evidence for upstream axonal damage.

Agreement on cytoskeletal defects (C53-C57). Both evaluations accept the Futsch staining data showing microtubule disruption. Peer reviewers affirm the authors 'demonstrate cytoskeletal and functional deficits' as part of the overall phenotype characterization, treating the quantitative data as valid.

Mixed evaluation of Wallerian degeneration independence (C67-C68). OpenEval finds the dSarm RNAi data 'effectively rules out Wallerian degeneration as the mechanism.' Peer reviewers show mixed views: one accepts it highlights different mechanisms, but another states 'important controls for these negative results are lacking,' indicating uncertainty.

OpenEval evaluates basic molecular identity and evolutionary context (C1-C4) as well-supported by literature and genomic data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these foundational characterization claims.

OpenEval supports the contextualization claim (C30) about Perlecan's maintenance role being consistent with literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this interpretive claim.
OpenEval evaluates comparative literature context (C70-C76) as well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/contextual claims.

OpenEval supports the synthesis about multi-cellular Perlecan contribution (C77-C78) based on cell-type experiments and literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this mechanistic inference.

OpenEval evaluates the inference about NMJ not being primary site of action (C79-C81) as reasonable given mechanical stress data and lack of synaptic enrichment. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific mechanistic interpretation.

OpenEval supports the mechanistic model synthesis (C82-C86) about catastrophic breakdown from neural lamella defects. While peer reviewers support the overall model (R12), they don't separately evaluate this specific mechanistic synthesis.

OpenEval evaluates mechanistic context from literature (C87-C89) about pathways linking ECM defects to neuronal dysfunction as plausible but untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these speculative mechanism claims.

OpenEval supports human disease context claims (C90-C91) as well-cited and establishing clinical relevance. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these translational context claims.
